When Liangda Hu first tried doing Daf Yomi, the practice of studying a page of Talmud per day, he struggled to read it. Hu found the language of English Talmud translations uniquely archaic and, as someone who speaks English as a second language, difficult to understand. Now, Hu uses ChatGPT to translate his daily Talmud study into his native Mandarin. “I think it’s quite reliable when it comes to translation,” he said. The technology is not perfect, Hu pointed out. To be safe, he often cross-references ChatGPT’s answers when asking about customs, like how to prepare for a particular fast day. AI is not the first technology to help Hu along his journey from his hometown in China toward becoming a Jew in his adopted home of Brownstone Brooklyn, where the 38-year-old immigrant has gone by the name Leo. Along the way, a broadcast of “Fiddler on the Roof” and a Facebook connection with his first Jewish friend played pivotal roles. Hu had no idea as a child in Tianjin, China, that he would ever be engaging with a Jewish language, or becoming one of the first — if not the first — daily Talmud students to work from a machine translation into Mandarin. Growing up just a decade removed from the Cultural Revolution, during which religion was essentially banned, would have made a future as a Jew in New York City feel like a farfetched possibility — if he could even have imagined it. But that was before Hu saw “Fiddler on the Roof.” “It was quite fascinating,” said Hu, who today lives in Prospect Heights while pursuing an MBA at Monroe College. He first watched the Academy Award-winning musical — a staple of the Ashkenazi Jewish cultural canon — while studying acting at a theater school in China. “What deeply fascinates me is how this family finds balance between tradition and an ever-changing reality,” Hu said, adding that he was also moved by “the way that Tevye expresses his relationship with God.” The musical had a profound effect on Hu, who moved to New York in 2021. Now, he is pursuing two simultaneous goals: to run his own theater company, and to officially convert to Judaism. Read more about Hu and his journey to Judaism at the link in our bio. 🎻

After all the solo trips to the bathroom with dozens of pies, and my make-believe Pie Girl, spanning decades; reality now replaced what I thought my imagination had cursed me with. Ansh Singh

It hurts in places you can’t explain. Not because he left, but because he left like it was easy. Like the late-night calls, the trembling I-love-yous, the way you showed up for him without needing to be asked—meant absolutely nothing. And what aches the most is knowing he doesn’t wonder about you at all. He’s not losing sleep, he’s not checking your stories, he’s not sitting quietly with your name echoing in his head. But you? You carry his memory like a wound you keep pressing on, just to see if it still hurts. And it always does. You still think maybe one day he’ll realize what you were to him. But darling, someone who truly cared would never put you in a position where you had to question your worth. He doesn’t miss you. Not your voice, not your laugh, not the way you loved him like he was made of poetry and fragility. He moved on—quietly, completely, and without a backward glance. And here you are, breaking your own heart every time you reread those old messages or stare at a timestamp that says Read 18:24. That’s not love. That’s you begging your past to feel something for a version of you he already forgot. You have to stop calling it love when it’s actually self-destruction. Stop giving him the power to define whether or not you were worth remembering. You were. You still are. And I know letting go feels like betrayal to the part of you that still hopes—but staying stuck in that grief is a slow death of your own light. He forgot you. That’s the truth. But now it’s your turn to remember yourself. The girl who loved deeply, gave freely, stayed quietly, and still believes in a kind of love that doesn’t walk away when it’s most needed. Hold onto that belief. Just don’t keep handing it to someone who didn’t even try to hold on to you.

OKAY SO I competed at the @akaiconofficial lip sync contest for the first time and learned a LOT of lessons. a lot of things went wrong on stage, but the outpouring of love and support i received from friends and strangers alike was unlike anything i’ve ever expected from a performance like this. hell, even the judges and participants had amazing things to say to me afterwards. thank you to everyone who supported me, it really inspired me to keep performing and doing what i love even when unexpected things happen in order: my wig fell off, pants ripped, notebook turned to wrong page, and after the performance i couldn’t help but cry and my whole ass (prescription) contact just popped out. i have extremely poor vision, so the entire time after the performance was a little difficult for me LOL it took a long time to process everything that happened, but i want to share my experience in hopes that people who are afraid to perform can see that just about anything can be turned around and made good, even if it feels like everything went wrong. thank you @belle.cosplay , @yotaku_boi and @liz.ard.cos for the recording and for cheering me on :3 special thanks to @pixiecosplays for talking me through the ENTIRE time. 🫶🫶 horns made by @maddenchaotic_cos #cosplay #helluva #helluvabossblitzø #helluvaboss #blitzo #blitzocosplay
